589.title: Life wasted without praise
589.hook: gun gobind gaaio nahee: if you haven't sung His praises, your life is wasted (Salok M9 1, ang 1426)
589.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the very end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, at the bhog ceremony that closes it, often held for weddings, new homes and funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kamal: love like a lotus, without clutching. Today, the last pages of the Granth, and the ninth Guru's saloks.

At the end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, after days of continuous recitation, the reader reaches the last few pages. The family who arranged the reading is often sitting close, sometimes after a wedding, sometimes after a death. What's read near the very end is a run of short couplets by Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Salok Mahalla nine. So these lines are heard at the turning points of Sikh family life. The first one is a single breath long, and it doesn't waste a word.
screen: `THE END OF A COMPLETE READING.` → `THE FAMILY SITTING CLOSE.` → `THE FIRST SALOK.`

segments.voice: The first salok begins gun gobind gaaio nahee, janam akaarath keen. In paraphrase: you haven't sung the praises of the Lord of the world; you've made your life useless. Gun means virtues, qualities. Gobind is the Lord who sustains the world. Gaaio is sung. And akaarath is for nothing, to no purpose, close cousin to the akaaj of Jaijavanti. Then the second line, in paraphrase: says Nanak, O mind, love the Lord the way a fish loves water. Stop on that fish. A fish doesn't visit the water now and then, or praise it once a week. Water is where it breathes. Take it out, and it gasps. That's the kind of praise the salok means: not a polite compliment, but the thing you can't live without. Notice the verb, too: sung. Sikh devotion is deeply musical. The Granth is set in ragas, kirtan fills the gurdwara, and praise here is often literally singing. The salok doesn't call a life without praise evil. It calls it akaarath, unused, like an instrument left in its case. And it's addressed to the mind, man, not to someone else. The Guru isn't scolding a crowd; he's speaking quietly to the inner voice of whoever is listening. Sikhs commonly count fifty-seven of these saloks, and many more are coming in the days ahead: short, steady, and very honest about time. The first one sets the tone.
screen: `GUN GOBIND GAAIO NAHEE.` · `AKAARATH: A LIFE UNUSED.` · `LIKE A FISH LOVES WATER.` · `PRAISE HERE IS SUNG.` · then, large: `SING, WHILE THERE'S TIME.`

segments.voice: If you know a shabad, or even just Waheguru, sing or hum it softly now, once or several times, without worrying about your voice; if singing feels strange, hum one long note and feel it in your chest. If you don't pray, sing a line of anything that makes you grateful, then sit and feel what's left in the body after the sound.
Gun, virtues, qualities. The first salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur says a life that never sings the Lord's gun goes unused, and asks the mind to love the Lord like a fish loves water.
Your line: sing, while there's time. Like a fish in water: not a visit, a home. Day five hundred eighty-nine, sung.

590.title: The days slip by
590.hook: the early saloks warn that days slip away while the mind sleeps (Salok M9, ang 1426)
590.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the ninth Guru's saloks at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; many know their refrain, kaho naanak, by heart, and take them as reminders that life's time is passing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gun: sing, while there's time. Today the saloks look straight at the time itself.

Look at a photo from five years ago. The haircut, the phone in your hand, the people beside you. Some you still see. Some you haven't spoken to in years. Where did those five years go? You were there for every day, and yet most of them left no trace. You weren't asleep. You were busy. But busy can be its own kind of sleep. The early saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur keep coming back to this, couplet after couplet, like someone gently shaking a sleeper's shoulder.
screen: `A PHOTO FROM FIVE YEARS AGO.` → `WHERE DID THE DAYS GO?` → `BUSY CAN BE A KIND OF SLEEP.`

segments.voice: The second salok asks, in paraphrase: why are you so absorbed in poisonous things? You don't turn away from them even for an instant. Says Nanak, meditate on the Lord, O mind, and you won't be caught in death's noose. The word for instant is nimakh, the blink of an eye. The salok isn't asking for a whole life of retreat. It asks: could you look up, even for one blink? The third salok ends with a line that sums up this whole run: your lifespan is passing, slipping away. Auadh is the span of life, the time you were given. And it's going, right now, at exactly the speed of this sentence. Listen to how the saloks repeat themselves. Again and again, the second line begins kaho naanak, says Nanak, and then calls the mind: O mind, man re, manaa. They're built like a refrain, and the repetition is the teaching. A single warning is forgotten by lunchtime. A couplet that keeps coming back, at the end of every reading, wears a groove in you. And notice what they don't say. They don't say the days are bad, or that time spent working or loving is wasted. They say the days slip, and the mind sleeps through them. The cure isn't more hours. It's waking up inside the ones you have, even for the blink of an eye.
screen: `WHY SO ABSORBED IN POISON?` · `NIMAKH: ONE BLINK OF AN EYE.` · `AUADH: THE LIFESPAN SLIPPING.` · `KAHO NAANAK: A REFRAIN THAT WAKES.` · then, large: `THE DAYS SLIP.`

segments.voice: Look at a clock and say the time to yourself, then the date, the day of the week, and where you are. Close your eyes and let each breath be a blink of waking, a nimakh; when you drift into plans or replays, come back to the clock's simple fact: it's now. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.
Auadh, the span of life. Guru Tegh Bahadur's early saloks warn that it is slipping away, and ask the mind to wake even for a blink.
Your line: the days slip. One awake blink is enough to begin. Five hundred ninety days, and counting.

591.title: None of it is yours
591.hook: wealth, spouse, property: you call them yours, but none goes with you (Salok M9, ang 1426)
591.howItsDone: The Sikh path is a householder's path of work, owning and sharing; the ninth Guru's salok on wealth, spouse and property is heard among his saloks at the bhog of a complete reading, including readings held after a death, as a reminder that nothing we own goes with us.

segments.voice: Yesterday, auadh: the span of life, slipping by. If the days are slipping, what are we holding as they go? Today's salok asks about the word mine.

Clearing out a parent's house after they've died is a strange job. Every drawer is full of things that mattered to someone. The good china saved for guests who rarely came. A box of receipts from 1987. A coat that still smells like them. Each object was mine to someone for decades. Now it's a question: keep, give, throw away. And the one who called it all mine isn't here to decide. Guru Tegh Bahadur's fifth salok stands in exactly that room.
screen: `CLEARING OUT A PARENT'S HOUSE.` → `EVERY DRAWER WAS SOMEONE'S MINE.` → `THE FIFTH SALOK.`

segments.voice: The salok begins dhan daaraa sampat sagal, jin apunee kar maan. In paraphrase: wealth, spouse, all your property, all the things you take to be your own: not one of them is your companion. Says Nanak, know this as true. Dhan is wealth. Sampat is property. Daaraa is wife, or spouse. And the key phrase is apunee kar maan: to treat as one's own. That's what the salok is really looking at: not the things, but the word mine stamped on them. Listing a spouse beside the money can sound harsh. But the Sikh path is lived in families; the ninth Guru himself was a husband and father. The salok isn't saying don't love your husband or wife. It's saying that even the person closest to you isn't a possession, and doesn't travel with you through death. Heard that way, it's almost tender. The people we love were never ours to own. They were gifts, given for a while. And notice the word companion, sangee. The salok isn't asking you to throw anything away. It's asking: who walks with you all the way? On day five hundred twelve, Sukhmani said the earned Name and the self your deeds shaped are what go along. This couplet makes the same point from the other side, by naming what stays behind. The result is a lighter grip. You can enjoy a good house, love a family, earn honestly, and still say quietly: this is lent to me.
screen: `DHAN, DAARAA, SAMPAT.` · `APUNEE KAR MAAN: CALLING IT MINE.` · `PEOPLE AREN'T POSSESSIONS.` · `WHAT IS LENT, NOT OWNED.` · then, large: `NONE OF IT GOES.`

segments.voice: Pick up something you own and care about, a ring, a watch, a mug, your phone, and hold it in an open hand, feeling its weight and thinking about where it came from. Say quietly to yourself, this is lent to me, and notice whether the grip tightens or loosens; then put it down gently and sit with empty hands. If you pray, you can give thanks to Waheguru for what's been lent.
Meraa, mine. The fifth salok loosens the grip of this word: wealth, spouse and property, everything we call meraa, is not our companion all the way; know this as true.
Your line: none of it goes. Mine gets quieter when you hear it as lent. Until tomorrow.

592.title: The Lord in every heart
592.hook: ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai: the Lord dwells in every heart, as the holy proclaim (Salok M9, ang 1427)
592.howItsDone: Sikhs serve langar to anyone who comes, seated together on the floor, and remember Bhai Ghanaiya, who gave water to the wounded on both sides, as a model of seeing the Lord in every heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, meraa: none of it goes; what we call mine is lent. So what is truly near? Today's salok answers.

Sikh tradition tells of a man named Bhai Ghanaiya. During the battles around Anandpur, he carried a water skin across the battlefield and gave water to the wounded, to Sikhs and to the soldiers they were fighting. Some Sikhs were furious and brought him before Guru Gobind Singh. The Guru asked him why he was helping the enemy. Bhai Ghanaiya is remembered as answering that he saw no enemy: in every face, he saw only the Guru. The Guru, the story says, gave him ointment as well, and told him to bandage their wounds too.
screen: `BHAI GHANAIYA'S WATER SKIN.` → `WATER FOR BOTH SIDES.` → `IN EVERY FACE, THE GURU.`

segments.voice: His answer echoes today's salok, written by Guru Gobind Singh's own father. Ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai, santan kahio pukaar. In paraphrase: the Lord dwells in every heart; the holy ones have proclaimed it aloud. Then: says Nanak, meditate on Him, O mind, and you'll cross the terrifying ocean. Ghatt means a clay pot, a vessel, and from that, the body or heart that holds a life. Ghatt ghatt: pot after pot, every single vessel. Not just the devout or the kind, or our own people. Every vessel. And pukaar is a loud call, a shout: the holy haven't whispered this. Last week, in the forest hymn, the Lord was within like scent in a flower; that was about finding God inside yourself. This salok turns the same teaching outward. Every vessel means mine, and yours, and the stranger's, and the soldier's on the other side. That's what makes it hard. Seeing God in the people we love comes more easily. The salok doesn't stop there. Sikhs see the same line at work in langar, which feeds anyone who walks in, of any faith or none, seated together on the floor. Seva, service, isn't reserved for members either. And Bhai Ghanaiya's water skin is what the line looks like when someone lives it.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you find difficult, not your worst enemy, just someone who annoys you or whom you've written off, and picture the salok's clay vessel. You don't have to like them; let the thought sit, the Lord dwells here too, and notice what softens and what resists. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru for one breath.
Ghatt, a vessel, the heart. Ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai: the salok says the Lord lives in every ghatt, every heart, as the holy proclaim aloud.
Your line: in every heart. Every heart includes the ones on the other side. That's day five hundred ninety-two.

593.title: Untouched by pain and pleasure
593.hook: the one untouched by pleasure, pain, greed, attachment and pride is the Lord's image (Salok M9, ang 1427)
593.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok among the ninth Guru's saloks at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and often cite it to say that a person free of craving and pride shows the image of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghatt: the Lord lives in every heart. Today's salok says what it looks like when that light shines through.

Someone stands at the bakery counter at the end of a long day. The smell hits. The craving arrives like a wave: just one, you deserve it, it's been a terrible afternoon. They stand there. And sometimes, if they simply wait, something surprising happens. The wave crests, and then it falls. Thirty seconds later, the want is smaller. Two minutes later, it's gone. From the inside, a craving can feel permanent. This one wasn't. The thirteenth salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur describes a person these waves can't knock over, and then gives that person a startling name.
screen: `THE BAKERY COUNTER.` → `A CRAVING, LIKE A WAVE.` → `IT CRESTS, THEN FALLS.`

segments.voice: The salok says, in paraphrase: the one whom pleasure and pain don't touch, nor greed, attachment or pride: says Nanak, listen, O mind, that one is the very image of God. The key verb is parsai, to touch, to brush against. These waves come to everyone. The salok doesn't say this person never meets pleasure or pain, greed or pride. They come and don't stick, like rain running down a window while the glass stays clear. Then the startling name: moorat bhagvaan, the image of God. Moorat means a form, an image, the word used for statues in temples. Sikhs don't worship images. And yet here, in the last pages of the Granth, the ninth Guru uses that very word for a living person: not stone, but a human being whose heart isn't pushed around. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Granth, calls God akaal moorat, the form beyond time. The same word. There it describes the Timeless; here, a person clear enough to show it. And it builds on yesterday. The salok before this one said the Lord lives in every heart. In this picture, the waves of craving and pride cover that light, the way waves cover the sand. When they settle, it shows. So becoming untouched isn't about becoming hard. It's about becoming clear, so the One already inside can be seen.
screen: `PARSAI: THE WAVES DON'T STICK.` · `MOORAT BHAGVAAN: GOD'S IMAGE.` · `AKAAL MOORAT, THE SAME WORD.` · `CLEAR ENOUGH TO SHOW THE LIGHT.` · then, large: `UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe, and wait for any want to arise, to check your phone, to snack, to move; when it comes, don't act and don't fight, just watch it like a wave, rising, cresting, beginning to fall, and count the breaths it takes. You're practicing being touched without being moved. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.
Moorat, a form, an image. The thirteenth salok calls the one whom pleasure, pain, greed, attachment and pride don't touch moorat bhagvaan, the very image of God.
Your line: untouched. Not hard, just clear enough for the light to show. See you tomorrow.

594.title: Gold and iron alike
594.hook: the one to whom praise and blame, gold and iron are the same (Salok M9, ang 1427)
594.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the fourteenth salok among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and speak of jeevan mukat, being free while alive, as its ideal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, moorat: untouched by the waves inside, clear enough to show God's image. Today, the voices outside.

A performance review lands in your inbox. Four paragraphs of praise, and one line that says you could communicate more clearly. Guess which line gets replayed on the drive home. The praise fades by dinner; the criticism rides along like a stone in a shoe. Or the reverse: one big compliment and you float for days, and then you need another. Either way, someone else's voice is holding the steering wheel. Guru Tegh Bahadur's fourteenth salok describes a person who has taken the wheel back.
screen: `FOUR PARAGRAPHS OF PRAISE.` → `ONE LINE ON THE DRIVE HOME.` → `WHO HOLDS THE WHEEL?`

segments.voice: The salok begins ustat nindiaa naahi jih, kanchan loh samaan. In paraphrase: the one for whom there is no praise and no slander, to whom gold and iron are the same: says Nanak, listen, O mind, know that one to be liberated. Ustat is praise. Nindiaa is slander, blame, talking someone down. Kanchan is gold, and loh is iron, the everyday metal of pots and plows. Samaan is equal, alike. The salok doesn't say this person never gets praised or blamed. Praise and blame just have no hook to catch on. Then it sets two metals side by side. Gold glitters; it's what we'd like to be called. Iron is ordinary. The salok asks for the same calm when someone calls you iron as when someone calls you gold. Back on day five hundred eighty-two, in a Sorath hymn, gold and dust were seen alike. Here it's gold and iron. The ninth Guru keeps returning to this picture, as if it's worth hearing more than once. And notice the last word: mukat, liberated. Sikh teaching speaks of jeevan mukat, someone free while still alive. Freedom here isn't a place you go after death. It's a person at a desk, reading a review, who can take the praise and the one line of criticism with the same steady face, learn from both, and stay themselves. Not to stop hearing what people say, but to stop being steered by it.

595.title: Fear none, frighten none
595.hook: bhai kaahoo kau det neh neh bhai maanat aan: frighten no one and fear no one; that one is wise (Salok M9, ang 1427)
595.tomorrow: Like a dream and a show
595.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom each year, especially at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, and often recite his salok on giving and taking no fear as the heart of his example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kanchan: praise and blame, gold and iron, met with the same steady face. Today, a salok many Sikhs link to his life.

Think of two kinds of people who make a room go tense. One is the bully: loud, threatening, used to getting their way by making others afraid. The other is so afraid themselves that they'll agree to anything, betray anyone, to stay safe. They look like opposites. But they're often the same person on different days. Fear going out and fear coming in are two ends of one rope. Guru Tegh Bahadur's sixteenth salok cuts that rope at both ends, in a single line.
screen: `THE BULLY AND THE FRIGHTENED.` → `TWO ENDS OF ONE ROPE.` → `ONE LINE CUTS BOTH.`

segments.voice: The salok says bhai kaahoo kau det neh, neh bhai maanat aan. In paraphrase: the one who gives fear to no one, and accepts fear from no one else: says Nanak, listen, O mind, call that one wise. Bhai is fear. Det is to give. Maanat is to accept, to take on. The wise one, giaanee, is defined by both at once. Sikhs hear this beside two words from the Mool Mantar: nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without enmity. Those describe God. This salok describes a person who has started to resemble them. And Sikhs think of the man who wrote it. Sikh tradition remembers that in 1675, a group of Kashmiri Pandits, Hindus, came to him at Anandpur. They said Mughal officials were forcing them to give up their faith. He listened, and set out for Delhi himself. He raised no army. He threatened no one. On the way he was arrested and taken to Delhi. When he was ordered to give up his own faith or die, he refused. He was executed in Delhi, at the place where Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands today. Sikhs call him Hind di Chadar, the shield of India, and remember that he gave his life for the freedom of people whose faith was not his own. He didn't frighten his enemies, and he didn't let them frighten him. That's a very hard kind of courage, gentle and brave in the same moment, and the salok makes it sound almost simple.
screen: `BHAI: NOT GIVEN, NOT TAKEN.` · `NIRBHAU, NIRVAIR.` · `ANANDPUR TO DELHI, 1675.` · `HIND DI CHADAR.` · then, large: `FRIGHTEN NONE, FEAR NONE.`

segments.voice: Think of one situation coming up where fear might show up on either end, where you might lean on someone too hard or give in when you shouldn't: a meeting, a family conversation, a moment of standing up for someone. Picture yourself in it, speaking calmly and clearly, neither pushing nor shrinking, and feel your feet on the floor. If you pray, you can ask Waheguru for that steadiness.
Fear none. The sixteenth salok calls wise the one who frightens no one and accepts fear from no one, and Sikhs see it lived in Guru Tegh Bahadur's walk to Delhi.
Your line: frighten none, fear none. Neither pushing nor shrinking: the rope cut at both ends. Rest well tonight.
